title: The Protection Diode That Starved the 5 V Sensor
featured_title: THE PROTECTION DIODE THAT STARVED THE 5 V SENSOR
subject: electrical-computer
audience: FE Electrical and Computer candidates and engineering students

presentation.challenge: The reverse-polarity protection worked, but the 5 V sensor would not start.

practice.primary_question: Why can a forward-biased protection diode make a downstream 5 V sensor fail even though the source is correct?
practice.typical_exam_trap: Treating a forward-biased silicon diode as a perfect zero-volt short when supply margin matters.

case_dna.target_misconception: Treating every conducting diode as a zero-volt ideal short.
case_dna.why_plausible: A familiar simplified electronics relation is easy to apply without checking the assumptions that make it valid.
case_dna.contradicting_evidence: With the 0.7 V constant-drop model, the resistor sees 4.3 V, so current is 4.3 mA, not 5 mA.
case_dna.corrected_model: Check the device model and operating region first, then apply the corresponding circuit equation.

problem_statement: A 5.0 V source feeds a sensor through a series silicon diode for reverse-polarity protection. The sensor requires at least 4.5 V to start. With a 0.7 V forward-drop model, only 4.3 V reaches the sensor.
fixed_constraints: Use the stated FE-style device model
Keep the stated source and main component values

gates.heading: The Diode That Wasn't a Short Circuit
facts: A 5 V source drives a forward-biased silicon diode and a 1 kΩ resistor in series. Using a 0.7 V silicon forward-drop model, the measured current is about 4.3 mA rather than the 5 mA ideal-short estimate.
gates.prompt: Why does a forward-biased silicon diode branch carry less current than an ideal-short model predicts?
